strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: selecting a segmentation model from a model zoo without target labels, source data, or fine-tuning. The microscopy motivation is compelling, and extending transferability estimation to instance segmentation is potentially useful.

CTE is simple and computationally attractive, requiring only an unperturbed and a perturbed inference pass. The distinction between black-box input perturbations and grey-box feature perturbations broadens its applicability.

The evaluation covers semantic and instance segmentation across several microscopy datasets and modalities. Reported rank correlations are strong, especially for feature perturbations, and the perturbation-strength sweep provides some evidence of robustness.
The manuscript is concise and generally clear, with an intuitive presentation of the core consistency hypothesis. Algorithms/General is the appropriate contribution type.
weaknesses: Consistency does not intrinsically measure correctness: a model producing a stable but systematically wrong, constant, empty, or full mask can receive an excellent CTE score. Foreground-union restriction does not resolve this issue and is undefined for two empty predictions. The paper supplies neither a theoretical condition nor stress tests with such failure cases, so the central estimator is insufficiently validated.

The experimental model banks are small—only three models per mitochondrial target and five to seven elsewhere—and mostly consist of U-Nets trained by the authors with similar losses, architectures, augmentations, and dropout. The exact perturbations used at evaluation were also used during training. Consequently, the strong correlations may reflect this tightly controlled training recipe rather than general model transferability. Only two public models are included, and there is no broad test across architectures, training pipelines, or modern pretrained/foundation models.

The comparison is inadequate for a state-of-the-art claim. CCFV estimates supervised fine-tuning transferability, which the authors acknowledge is a different objective, while relevant simple baselines such as predictive entropy/confidence, foreground statistics, Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty, or source/target feature-distribution measures are absent. No baseline at all is evaluated for instance segmentation.

Important protocol details are missing: the selected input transformation or mixture and its parameter values, dropout rate used for the main tables, how perturbation strength is chosen without labels, target sample counts, instance postprocessing, threshold selection, and the alpha value in the foreground Rand score. It is therefore unclear whether hyperparameters were fixed globally or selected using target-label performance.

The statistical evidence is weak. Correlations are averaged over few targets without confidence intervals or significance tests; perfect correlation with three models is not very informative. Results for each target/model bank, top-1 selection accuracy or regret, sensitivity to target-set size, random perturbation variance, and multiple training seeds are not reported.

The perturbation sweep covers only one target for each task and only feature dropout. The claim that one stochastic perturbation is sufficient is asserted without quantitative comparisons or variance estimates, while input perturbations—the black-box setting of greatest practical relevance—perform substantially worse for cell instance segmentation.

Reproducibility is limited by sparse training and evaluation details and no stated code/model-release plan. The discussion is exceptionally brief and does not analyze failure modes, computational measurements, domain scope, or limitations. Overall, the idea has merit, but consequential experimental and methodological gaps prevent a convincing ECCV-level case.

strengths: The paper targets a practical and relevant problem: selecting a segmentation model for an unlabeled microscopy dataset without accessing source data or fine-tuning on target labels.

The proposed consistency-based estimator is intuitive, inexpensive—requiring one perturbed and one unperturbed inference pass—and accommodates both black-box input perturbations and grey-box feature perturbations.

The evaluation covers semantic and instance segmentation, several microscopy tasks, and multiple public datasets. The reported rank correlations are often strong, especially for feature perturbations.
The perturbation-strength experiment is useful and suggests that the ranking is not tied to one exact dropout probability within the tested examples.
weaknesses: The evidence is too limited for the broad model-zoo and state-of-the-art claims. Most candidates are closely related 2D U-Nets trained by the authors under a common recipe; only two external models are mentioned. Each ranking contains just 3, 5, or 7 models, so apparently impressive correlations—particularly perfect ranking among three mitochondrial models—are statistically fragile and do not establish performance across heterogeneous architectures, training procedures, or real model zoos.

There is a serious evaluation confound: the source models are trained with the same categories of augmentation and dropout later used to perturb them. CTE may therefore measure robustness to transformations explicitly encouraged during training rather than general zero-shot transferability. Experiments with unseen perturbations and independently obtained models are necessary.

The only named baseline, CCFV, addresses supervised, fine-tuned transferability and has access to target labels. The manuscript itself acknowledges this mismatch, making the comparison unsuitable for substantiating the claimed new state of the art. Simple relevant baselines such as predictive entropy/confidence, foreground prevalence, alternative test-time consistency scores, and model-agreement or domain-distance measures are absent; no baseline is provided for instance segmentation.

Several essential methodological details are missing or ambiguous. The paper does not specify the input-perturbation parameter values, an operational label-free rule for selecting perturbation strength, the foreground threshold, the Rand-score parameter alpha, handling of empty predicted unions, instance-generation post-processing, or the precise mAP definition. Dataset-specific splits, source-target pairings, training hyperparameters, and per-pair numerical results are also insufficiently documented. No code or reproducibility artifact is identified.

The statistical presentation is weak. Results are averages and standard deviations of correlations over a small number of related target datasets, without confidence intervals or significance analysis. The same models and datasets are reused across transfers, undermining independence. Pearson correlation is also described as being computed between rankings, while it appears to be computed from raw estimator and performance values. Scatter plots often fit lines to only three to seven points.

The robustness study is narrow: Figure 3 examines dropout strength on only one target example per setting, while no comparable sweep is reported for the four input perturbations. The paper states that multiple perturbation samples offer no benefit but supplies no quantitative ablation supporting that assertion.

The proposed semantic hard score is essentially IoU between perturbed and unperturbed predictions, and the broader premise of perturbation consistency as a generalization proxy is inherited from prior work. Extending this idea to segmentation is potentially useful, but the technical novelty is modest and is not accompanied by theory explaining when consistency should preserve the true performance ordering or when confidently wrong models will rank highly.

Important failure modes are not investigated. A model can be stably wrong, predict overly smooth masks, or collapse to nearly constant foreground/background predictions while remaining highly consistent. Restricting evaluation to the predicted foreground union does not resolve all such degeneracies, and no adversarial controls, qualitative failures, or out-of-scope cases are presented.

The discussion largely restates the claimed success and does not meaningfully address limitations, sensitivity to target-set size, computational measurements, domain-specific perturbation choices, calibration, or generalization beyond microscopy and binary U-Net-style segmentation. Overall, the idea has merit, but consequential experimental and reproducibility gaps prevent a convincing acceptance case.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: selecting a segmentation model from a model zoo using only an unlabeled target dataset, without source data or fine-tuning.
The proposed consistency-based transferability estimator is simple, intuitive, computationally lightweight, and supports both black-box input perturbations and grey-box feature perturbations.

The extension to instance segmentation is valuable and comparatively underexplored. The evaluation covers semantic and instance segmentation across nuclei, cells, and mitochondria from multiple microscopy modalities.

The reported ranking correlations are promising. Feature-based CTE achieves average Kendall tau values of 1.00 for mitochondrial semantic segmentation, 0.83 for nuclei semantic segmentation, 0.87 for cell instance segmentation, and 0.76 for nuclei instance segmentation.
The comparison between soft and hard consistency metrics is informative, and the perturbation-strength sweep provides useful evidence that the ranking is not tied to one exact dropout rate.
The manuscript is concise and generally clear, and the two-inference-run implementation could be useful in practical model-bank settings.
weaknesses: The empirical scale is limited at the level most relevant to the claim: each ranking contains only 3–7 models. Correlations, especially perfect correlations for three-model banks, can therefore look impressive despite being based on very few pairwise ordering decisions. Confidence intervals, significance tests, or per-target results are not provided.

Baseline coverage is inadequate. CCFV is designed for supervised, fine-tuned transferability rather than the zero-shot setting and is therefore not a fully comparable baseline. The paper should evaluate simple unsupervised alternatives such as predictive entropy/confidence, foreground prevalence, output sharpness, or other uncertainty and augmentation-consistency scores. There is no baseline at all for instance segmentation.

Most evaluated models share a 2D U-Net architecture, training loss, augmentation family, and training pipeline; only two external models are mentioned. Consequently, the experiments do not establish robustness to the heterogeneous architectures, calibration properties, preprocessing conventions, or training recipes expected in a real model zoo.

The method requires choosing a domain-appropriate perturbation and its strength without target labels. Although a dropout sweep is shown for selected transfers, the paper gives no unsupervised selection rule and does not adequately test failure modes such as harmful or semantically invalid input transformations. Feature dropout also assumes access to and compatibility with an appropriate internal layer.

Reproducibility details are insufficient: exact dataset sizes and splits, preprocessing and normalization, perturbation parameters, prediction thresholds, instance post-processing, the value of alpha in the foreground-restricted Rand score, optimization settings, and implementation/code availability are not reported. The claim that multiple perturbation runs provide no advantage is asserted without quantitative evidence or variability over random perturbation draws.

The evaluation is confined to microscopy and largely to closely related U-Net models, yet the discussion makes broad state-of-the-art and model-bank claims. Testing diverse architectures and non-microscopy segmentation domains, or narrowing the claims, would strengthen the paper.

The formulation needs correction and clarification. Equation 5 uses awkward set/count notation for NHD while claiming equivalence to IoU, and the paper does not precisely specify how transformed predictions are aligned or inverted for all input perturbations. Empty-union cases also need an explicit convention.

The discussion is too brief and does not analyze likely failure cases—for example, a consistently wrong or near-constant predictor can be highly invariant—or limitations arising from different label conventions across source and target datasets. These issues weaken the causal interpretation that consistency reliably indicates transfer performance.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: selecting semantic or instance segmentation models without source data or labeled target data. The output-space formulation is particularly useful for comparing architectures with incompatible feature spaces and instance-formation pipelines.

The proposed CTE is simple, computationally attractive, and broadly applicable. Its input-perturbation variant can operate as a black-box method, while requiring only an unperturbed and a perturbed inference pass per image.

The empirical coverage is unusually broad for biomedical segmentation, spanning semantic and instance segmentation, 2D and 3D data, multiple imaging modalities and anatomical structures, domain-specific and generalist models, and post-UDA model selection.

Results are consistently promising: semantic-segmentation experiments report mean Kendall correlations around 0.62–0.77 across microscopy tasks, ToothFairy2 reaches 0.90–1.00 for several overall rankings, and instance segmentation achieves mean Kendall correlations of 0.69–0.80. CTE also substantially outperforms the unsupervised Transfer Score baseline.

The manuscript is clear about important failure modes, including stable all-background/all-foreground predictions, task misalignment such as cell-versus-nucleus switching, reduced reliability on VNC after UDA, and incompatibility with boundary-sensitive performance criteria.
weaknesses: The perturbation type, magnitude, and feature-injection location are free hyperparameters, but the paper does not provide a label-free selection rule or a held-out protocol for choosing them. Many settings are swept using labeled target performance, and the main tables report selected single settings without a clear pre-specified choice; this weakens the zero-shot deployment claim and creates a risk of optimistic reporting.

Several evaluations contain very small model banks—only five models for nuclei instance segmentation and seven for ToothFairy2—making correlations coarse and unstable. Many per-dataset rank correlations are statistically nonsignificant, especially for instance segmentation, despite favorable averages.

The central assumption that consistency implies correctness is structurally fragile. The documented collapsed-output, wrong-structure, and stable-confusion cases are not merely rare implementation problems: they directly contradict the estimator's signal. The suggested entropy or diversity correction is not implemented or evaluated.

The experimental design does not establish generalization of the ranking rule to unseen task families or non-biomedical imagery. Most model banks also share related U-Net-style architectures, training pipelines, or source datasets, so the breadth in datasets does not fully translate into independent evidence across model ecosystems.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: code is only promised, exact preprocessing and normalization needed to interpret perturbation magnitudes are insufficiently specified, some aggregation details such as class weights are unclear, and there are inconsistencies in reported model-set sizes (for example, the nuclei semantic-segmentation supplement reports both 7 and 12 models).

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: selecting biomedical segmentation models without source data or labeled target data. Extending transferability estimation to instance segmentation is particularly useful and comparatively underexplored.

CTE is simple, computationally attractive, and applicable through input perturbations with only two inference passes. Output-space comparison also permits ranking models with heterogeneous architectures and instance-formation procedures.

The evaluation spans semantic and instance segmentation, 2D and 3D data, several biomedical modalities, public generalist models, and post-UDA selection. Many reported rank correlations are encouraging, especially for mitochondrial semantic segmentation and ToothFairy2.

The manuscript clearly acknowledges genuine failure modes, including collapsed predictions, stable but incorrect segmentations, source-target task mismatch, and weak alignment with boundary-sensitive evaluation metrics.
weaknesses: The experimental protocol risks optimistic bias. Target datasets were explicitly selected partly because their ground-truth performance exhibited model differentiation, and several candidate banks include models trained on the same dataset as the target. The paper does not report correlations after excluding these in-domain models; such conspicuous high-performance points can substantially inflate Pearson correlation and make the intended cross-domain setting easier.

The practical objective is selecting the best model, but evaluation is almost entirely based on global correlation. No top-1 selection accuracy, selected-model regret, top-k recall, or comparison with an oracle is reported. Moderate correlation can still select the wrong best model, so the central model-selection claim is not fully demonstrated.

Perturbation type, magnitude, and injection location are additional hyperparameters requiring a label-free selection rule. The supplement sweeps many dataset-dependent settings, while the main tables do not clearly specify a universal precommitted configuration. Performance can vary materially across settings, including complete failure for some instance-segmentation cases, leaving open whether favorable configurations were selected using target labels.

The baseline study is incomplete and partly mismatched. Most semantic baselines are supervised classification-derived measures designed for a different setting, whereas simple unsupervised alternatives such as prediction entropy/confidence, foreground or instance-count statistics, conventional test-time-augmentation uncertainty, and combinations intended to detect collapsed outputs are absent. Instance segmentation is evaluated without any baseline, making the absolute value of CTE difficult to establish.

Statistical support is weaker than the summary language suggests. Candidate banks are small (only five models for nuclei instance segmentation and seven for several other experiments), many individual Kendall or Spearman correlations are not significant, and models sharing source datasets or architectures are treated as independent observations. Near-perfect Pearson values sometimes coexist with much weaker rank correlations, consistent with domination by one or two extreme models.

The method fails precisely for stable but confidently wrong predictions, including all-background/all-foreground collapse and segmentation of the wrong biological structure. These are not merely pathological edge cases in biomedical transfer. Although the paper proposes diversity or entropy as possible remedies, it does not implement or evaluate them.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the breadth of the study: training schedules, optimizers, learning rates, seeds, exact candidate-model composition, preprocessing details, and the fixed perturbation configuration are not fully specified, and code is only promised. There are also inconsistent reported model counts, such as seven nuclei models in Table 1 versus twelve in Table 20.

Overall, the central idea and results have merit, but under the default Algorithms/General contribution type the current evidence does not yet rule out selection bias or establish reliable deployment-time model selection. A held-out evaluation with a fixed perturbation policy, exclusion of in-domain candidates, stronger unsupervised baselines, and top-model regret metrics would be needed for acceptance.

The output-space formulation is well motivated and accommodates semantic and instance segmentation models with heterogeneous architectures and post-processing pipelines. The Adapted Rand Score formulation for instance segmentation is a particularly useful contribution because classification-derived estimators are not directly applicable there.

The empirical scope is strong: experiments cover mitochondria, nuclei, cells, and 42-class CBCT anatomy; semantic and instance segmentation; 2D and 3D data; multiple architectures; public generalist models; and post-UDA selection.

Results are consistently favorable. For semantic segmentation, CTE substantially outperforms the unsupervised Transfer Score baseline; on ToothFairy2 it obtains strong correlations across several class groups; and the instance-segmentation experiments generally show good monotonic and linear correlations.

The perturbation sweeps are valuable and show that performance is reasonably stable over broad ranges of Gaussian, gamma, brightness, contrast, and dropout strengths, reducing concern that the headline results depend on one narrowly tuned setting.

The manuscript is clear and unusually candid about failure modes, including collapsed predictions, stable but incorrect segmentations, cell-versus-nucleus mode switching, task misalignment, and weaker post-UDA results on VNC.
weaknesses: The practical evaluation reports correlation coefficients but not the downstream model-selection quantities users ultimately care about, such as top-1 selection accuracy, regret relative to the oracle model, or performance of the selected model. High global rank correlation does not ensure that the best model is selected correctly.

Several ranking sets are small—only five models for nuclei instance segmentation and seven for ToothFairy2—and many per-dataset correlations are not statistically significant. The paper lacks bootstrap confidence intervals over target images, repeated perturbation seeds, and robustness analysis for stochastic single-pass estimates.

The model banks for several experiments appear to include models trained on the same dataset distribution as the target, alongside genuinely cross-domain models. These in-domain models may provide easy ranking anchors and inflate correlations. Results excluding all same-dataset source models would better establish the claimed transfer setting.

Although perturbation sweeps are extensive, the manuscript does not give a fully label-free rule for choosing perturbation type and magnitude on a new dataset. Reporting a single universally fixed configuration across all tasks, or an unsupervised calibration criterion, would make deployment claims more convincing.

CTE fundamentally measures stability rather than correctness. The documented cases of all-background/all-foreground collapse, stable segmentation of the wrong structure, and erroneous post-UDA predictions are consequently structural limitations rather than rare implementation issues. A diversity or entropy safeguard is suggested but not evaluated.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript says code will be released, while key training settings, random seeds, normalization choices, thresholds, post-processing parameters, and the ARS weighting parameter are not fully specified. The experimental conclusions would be stronger with released code and exact configurations.

The novelty is primarily a careful extension and validation of perturbation consistency ideas rather than a deep new theoretical principle. The margin-based motivation is plausible, but no formal result explains when consistency should preserve performance rankings or characterize its failure conditions.
